prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The only result so far is the starting architecture, and it scored zero on both seeds. Its policy collapsed to choosing DONE at once: episode length fell to 1.0 by the halfway point of training. Random placements usually lose reward, so stopping immediately (return 0) is a local optimum the policy can fall into. It has to learn that placing on missing cells pays before DONE takes over.

The task has a clear structure. A brick lands at layer z when every cell under its footprint is empty at z and at least one has support at z−1. The placement is good when the target needs all of those cells at layer z. The starting network mixes all layers in a 1x1 stem, so it is hard for it to learn this per-layer check.

This round runs two by two: per-layer network vs starting network, default recipe vs a recipe with more, smaller updates and more entropy. One cell (starting network, default recipe) is the starting result, so three trials remain.

### Round 2
All 4 runs so far (including the starting net) collapsed to DONE, whatever the network or recipe. The untrained traces show why. Each placement lands mirrored in x. The fill starts at column X − dx − x, not x: 1x1 at col 2 fills col 5, 1x2 at col 6 fills cols 0–1, 2x2 at col 6 fills cols 0–1. Rows are unchanged, and the target is observed correctly. A conv head that scores the anchor cell (y, x) therefore scores the wrong place for every action. Placements look like random drops with negative reward, and DONE (reward 0) wins. Recipe changes cannot fix this. The fix is to wire the action space after the learned layers: flip each type's score map in x and shift it left by dx−1. Round 2 tests this wiring: candidate 1 is the starting net with the default recipe, candidate 2 adds a recipe with more updates, and candidate 3 is the per-layer net with that same recipe.

### Round 3
This world mirrors the x axis: action column x lands on observed columns X−dx−x to X−1−x. Without flipping the placement maps to match, every net collapsed to DONE and scored 0. With the flip, the start net got 0.669 on the default recipe and 0.898 (0.943 and 0.852 by seed) with 128 envs and 3 epochs, giving about 83 updates. More updates clearly helped: the gap is well beyond the seed spread. Training success was still rising at the end (0.876 at 75%, 0.902 at 100%), so the run looks short of updates and samples. The per-layer net learned more slowly and scored 0.21. The dev builds are nearly right (IoU 0.992, 0.25 cells outside the target per episode), so the remaining failures are probably ordering mistakes around overhangs or stopping too early. This round tests three single changes to r2c2: more samples and updates, longer credit assignment for the delayed +1 exact-build bonus, and global context passed back into the per-cell features.

### Round 4
Flipping each placement score map in x so it lines up with the action indices was the decisive change. Every trial without it collapsed to choosing DONE (0.0); with it the same start net reached 0.67 under the default recipe. More policy updates then raised this to 0.90 in r2c2, which used 128 envs, 3 epochs and 16 minibatches, giving 79 updates and about 3.8k gradient steps. The variants of r2c2 all did worse. Cutting to 2 epochs and 8 minibatches (r3c1) gave 0.07 with only about 1.8k gradient steps. Adding a global broadcast gave 0.86/0.40. Raising gamma to 0.99 gave 0.95 on one seed and 0.0 on the other. Results vary hugely between seeds, and one failure mode is a seed that never learns. The pattern so far is that more optimiser updates and gradient steps help. When the trained net does work, its failures are rare wrong cells (0.25 extra cells per episode), which points to how precisely the head judges each footprint. This round tests more gradient steps, more updates, and a deeper footprint head.

## Trial it ended with
name: r2c2 with 32 minibatches
hypothesis: Same as r2c2, with 32 minibatches instead of 16 (64 samples each). This doubles the gradient steps per update (about 7.6k in total) while keeping the samples and the 79 updates. r3c1 to r2c2 suggests that more gradient steps help. Refuted if 2-seed dev success is at or below 0.90, or a seed collapses.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).
